title: A hard hadith, read in context
hook: a hadith about fighting people until they testify, which scholars read as about the wars of its time, alongside no compulsion in religion
tomorrow: why avoid all of the wrong, but only some of the right?

segments.voice: Yesterday, nasihah: religion as sincere goodwill, to Allah and to people. Sincere goodwill. Today, goodwill is needed for a text that's easy to misuse.

After class, a ten-year-old holds up his big brother's phone. A clip: dark music, big white captions, a line from a hadith. I have been commanded to fight the people. Then it cuts to black. He doesn't ask what it means. He asks, quietly, whether it means he's supposed to hate his friend from soccer. Yesterday's question asked which hadith gets clipped and shared to scare people. This is the one, eighth in al-Nawawi's forty. And the clip stops right before the part that matters.
screen: `DARK MUSIC, WHITE CAPTIONS.` → `'DO I HAVE TO HATE MY FRIEND?'` → `THE CLIP STOPS TOO SOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole report from Ibn Umar, in paraphrase. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said he was commanded to fight the people until they testify that there's no god but Allah and that he is Allah's messenger, establish the prayer and give zakat; and if they do, their lives and property are safe, except by the right of Islam, and their reckoning is with Allah. Read in ten seconds, it sounds like a war on everyone. Now read it with the scholars. First: who are the people? Commentators read the word here as a particular group, those then at war with the Muslims, in the wars of its time, not all of humankind. Second: the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation. "There is no compulsion in religion." Another verse says Allah doesn't forbid kindness and fair dealing toward those who don't fight you over religion. The scholars read the hadith inside those verses, not against them. Third: the last line, the one the clip always cuts. Their reckoning is with Allah. Outward words are accepted, and no one gets to put a heart on trial. One to tell a friend tonight: a hard text read alone and the same text read with its scholars can be two different texts.
screen: `THE WHOLE REPORT.` · `'THE PEOPLE': THE WARS OF ITS TIME.` · `NO COMPULSION IN RELIGION.` · `THEIR RECKONING IS WITH ALLAH.` · then, large: `READ IT WITH THE SCHOLARS.`

segments.voice: Say the verse out loud, slowly, in Pickthall's words: "There is no compulsion in religion." Say it a second time, more quietly. Then sit with it beside the hard hadith, not cancelling it but holding it, the way the scholars hold the two together.
screen: `SAY IT OUT LOUD.` · `NO COMPULSION IN RELIGION.`

segments.voice: A hard hadith: a report that's easy to misread on its own. This one is read with its setting, its closing line, and the Qur'an's no compulsion in religion.
One line to carry: read it with the scholars, the whole report and its setting, never the clip alone. Ten days into the last range.

screen: `DAY 1436 COUNTS.` → `YEAR FIVE · 10 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: WHY AVOID ALL OF THE WRONG, BUT ONLY SOME OF THE RIGHT?`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers read hard hadith with the classical commentaries and the Qur'an's verses on the same subject, and explain a report's setting before its meaning is applied.

chat.meaning: The clip cuts the setting and the last line. Read with the scholars, it's about the wars of its time, beside 'no compulsion in religion'.

hadith.meaning: a report of what the Prophet said or did

Ibn Umar.meaning: Abdullah ibn Umar, a companion who reported this hadith

zakat.meaning: the yearly giving owed from wealth

Pickthall.meaning: Marmaduke Pickthall, an English Muslim who translated the Qur'an's meanings

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22 (Ibn Umar: commanded to fight the people until they testify… their reckoning is with Allah)

sources.quoted: There is no compulsion in religion.

sources.ref: Qur'an 60:8 (Allah does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who did not fight you over religion)

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): story shape; the scene is a child shown a clip that quotes this hadith. For parents: the lesson deals with a hadith about fighting; it stays non-graphic and centers the child's worry about a friend.

The reading of 'the people' (al-nas) as a particular group, those then at war with the Muslims, follows the outline ('scholars read it as about the wars of its time'); commentators differ on detail (some say the Arab polytheists of that time; others tie it to those who fight). A Keeper should confirm the phrasing is fair and not overstated.
Qur'an 2:256 quoted from Pickthall 1930; 60:8 paraphrased. Confirm both.
'Except by the right of Islam' is kept in the report but not explained (it refers to legal rights such as those in hadith 14, day 1442).
Gloss 'Pickthall: an English Muslim who translated the Qur'an's meanings' (Pickthall titled his work The Meaning of the Glorious Koran). Confirm.
